stages.title: Selling the Dream to Wall Street

parts.visual:
An IPO is when a private company sells its stock to the public for the first time. It is the ultimate goal of most startups.

The IPO Process:
1. The S-1 Filing: A brutal legal document revealing every financial secret and risk of the company to the public.
2. The Roadshow: The CEO and CFO travel for weeks, pitching the company to massive institutional investors to convince them to buy the stock.
3. Going Public: Ringing the bell on Wall Street and dealing with daily stock fluctuations.
parts.audio: An IPO is when a private company goes public. The CEO and CFO must execute a 'Roadshow' to convince massive institutional investors to buy their stock.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of an 'IPO Roadshow'?
options: To go on a fun vacation.
For the executive team to present their financial narrative to billionaires and pension funds, begging them to buy millions of shares before the stock opens to the public.
questions.correct_answer: For the executive team to present their financial narrative to billionaires and pension funds, begging them to buy millions of shares before the stock opens to the public.
questions.explanation: If the institutional investors hate the Roadshow pitch, the IPO will fail, the stock price will crash on day one, and the CEO will be fired.

questions.question: Listen to the SEC lawyer. What legal document is he demanding?
questions.tts_text: Before you can go public, you must file an S-1. It must list every single risk that could possibly destroy your company in the next ten years.
questions.explanation: The S-1 is a brutal requirement of transparency. You must publicly admit your weaknesses (e.g., 'We rely heavily on one supplier in China') so investors can't sue you later.

questions.question: What is the 'Quiet Period'?
options: A legally mandated period around an IPO where executives are strictly forbidden from talking to the press or hyping up the stock, to prevent market manipulation.
questions.correct_answer: A legally mandated period around an IPO where executives are strictly forbidden from talking to the press or hyping up the stock, to prevent market manipulation.
questions.explanation: If a CEO breaks the Quiet Period (e.g., by tweeting about how great the company is doing), the SEC can instantly halt the entire IPO.

questions.question: Why is becoming a public company sometimes considered a 'curse' for a CEO?
options: Because they lose their privacy and must cater to the short-term demands of Wall Street analysts every 90 days, instead of building long-term value.
Because they have to wear a suit.
questions.correct_answer: Because they lose their privacy and must cater to the short-term demands of Wall Street analysts every 90 days, instead of building long-term value.
questions.explanation: Going public makes you rich, but it costs you your freedom.
